So Im curious what all qualifies as punk. I sometimes exclude it from lists of genres I listen to because it's such an ambiguous description. I listen to a lot of Ramones, Iggy and the Stooges, Gogol Bordello and Velvet Underground. But they're all so completely different in style and intensity, it's tough to put them in a single genre.

I personally think punk is more of a mindset than a single type of music, but not everyone concurs with that assessment. Anyways what do you think?

Punk really is a very wide and ambiguous thing. As a life long listener to music and someone who is particularly fond of "punk," I have to say the one common idea is that to some extent it's counter culture or "against the grain." Oh, and usually quick tempo and usually leading with the drums, but that's technical stuff. My point: There are several qualities we can attribute to punk music, and without the right combination (some of this, but none of that) you can't really call it punk. For example, Metallica has fast and complex drum beats and is counter-culture, but it's certainly not punk. Gogol Bordello is maybe tangentially political and doesn't really have fast drumming, but is definitely gypsy punk.

It's hard to put your finger on it, unless you're talking about the Cali punk acts, while at the same time you can usually spot it right away.

That makes a lot of sense. I grew up in a town with a punk centric music scene. So I've heard a lot of elitist arguments as to what constitutes as punk or not. And no one can seem to agree.

But throughout them all there's always been some level of counter culture and a noticeable lack of fucks given.

I love going to punk shows, they always have the best atmosphere and mosh pits.

Punk. Damn it's so hard to talk about. In the beginning it was a term placed on a culture and music by outsiders. The people outside the scene deemed things "punk". But now it become a catchall for a shadowy reproduction of that original movement from the seventies.

Today, punk should be about a certain ethos and do it yourself mindset. An everything for everyone by anyone sort of culture. An anarchist economy with the goal of destroying the status quo. That was the point behind the punk movement. Jackets and Mohawks were just the media description of those people. Anything can be punk, it simply has to live up to that punk ethos and standard. Do it yourself. Fuck the status quo. Everything for everyone.

That's a good point. There's so many different kind of variations but they all have a similar mindset that you described.

I lived in a punk house for a year and that basically described how we operated. Everyone was on ebt, we provided for each other through bartering and good will. And had a great solidarity support situation worked out.

I agree that the Mohawks and leathers are more of a media tag that caught on and cemented itself. Sadly there's people out there that think that's a standard. I personally look like neither, more like a home bum or street kid to be honest. But damn I got the punk spirit alive in me, if I do say so myself.

So one thing I've always wondered, what in your opinion separates grunge from punk?

Grunge was more amorphous and inherently unoriginal. It was just a synthesis of the punk rock scene largely inhabited by middle class "slackers" looking for a movement. It was also co-opted and commercialized much quicker.

An interesting analysis I haven't heard before. Can't say I completely disagree either. However some of the same things can be said about the punk scene of the same era. I see quite a few similarities between the two. Perhaps it could be said the grunge scene of the 90's was just the punk scene of the 70's repackaged for a different generation.

Grunge was derivative of the original punk scene, but instead of DIY it was just Do. They made a small scene and it quickly went commercial. This is why it died so fast (both figuratively and literally in a few cases). Grunge started looking for the sellout and then got confused when it got it.

If it's got guitars, it's energetic, loud, and gets you pumping... then it's punk (most of the time). But i say it's more about attitude. When madonna came out with the video for 'like a prayer' and upset the vatican... that was a punk thing to do. If you try to challenge the 'norm' or what people believe by telling your version, then it's punk.
